questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: The Semiconservative Outcome
questions.learningObjective: describe what semiconservative replication produces
questions.stem: A diagram shows one parent DNA molecule as a two-stranded ladder. After a single round of replication the same diagram shows two molecules, and each one is drawn with a full-length dark strand matched to a full-length light strand. Which term describes that outcome?

options.text: Semiconservative replication, one old strand paired with one newly made strand
Conservative replication, one duplex with two old strands kept intact
options.misconception: believes the parental helix is copied whole and set beside a new helix

options.text: Dispersive replication, old and new bases mixed within both strands
options.misconception: believes new bases are scattered into the middle of each parental strand

options.text: Semiconservative replication, one duplex with two old strands kept together
options.misconception: names the right process while describing a whole-helix outcome

questions.explanation: Each product molecule in the diagram pairs a full-length old strand with a full-length new one, which is the definition of semiconservative replication, and it is what density-gradient experiments show. The tempting belief that the old helix stays whole fails because the two parental strands are separated at the fork, so neither can remain in the same molecule, and the belief that new bases are woven into the middle of old strands fails because each strand in the diagram is single-coloured from end to end.
questions.hint: Count the old strands in each product molecule, not the molecules.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Why a Primer Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: explain why a primer is required before DNA synthesis can start
questions.stem: A DNA polymerase can add a nucleotide only onto an existing three-prime end, so a short piece is laid down before the long chain is built. What is that starter piece, and why is it made of RNA?

options.text: An RNA primer, made by primase because the polymerase cannot start a strand
A DNA primer, made by primase because only DNA is ever copied
options.misconception: thinks copying always begins from a DNA template

options.text: A DNA primer, made by the polymerase to supply the first nucleotide
options.misconception: believes the polymerase can start a chain on its own

options.text: An RNA primer, made by the polymerase because RNA is copied first
options.misconception: assumes DNA is made through an RNA intermediate

questions.explanation: The building reaction needs a free three-prime end to attack the incoming nucleotide, and a fresh chain has none, so a short primer is laid down first by the separate enzyme primase, which synthesises RNA rather than DNA. That primer is disposable, being later cut out, replaced with DNA, and sealed. The tempting belief that the primer stays in the finished strand fails because a ribose base left in DNA reads as damage, and the belief that the polymerase can begin unaided fails because its active site has nothing to grip at the start.
questions.hint: Ask which enzyme, not which polymerase, makes the first piece.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Antiparallel Strands and Direction of Synthesis
questions.learningObjective: link the antiparallel strands to leading and lagging synthesis
questions.stem: The two strands of a duplex point in opposite directions along the molecule, and every DNA polymerase builds a new strand from its five-prime end towards its three-prime end. Which pair of statements about the two templates is correct?

options.text: The leading template is read three to five prime continuously, the lagging one in pieces
Both templates are read three to five prime continuously, so both strands grow in one piece
options.misconception: ignores that the two templates point in opposite directions

options.text: The leading template is read five to three prime continuously, the lagging one in pieces
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which a template is read

options.text: Both templates are read five to three prime, so the new strands must also grow that way
options.misconception: mixes up the direction of reading with the direction of building

questions.explanation: A polymerase reads its template three-prime to five-prime because that is the only direction in which the new strand's growing three-prime end can stay alongside the template, and it builds the new strand five-prime to three-prime. Because the templates are antiparallel, only one is oriented so the new strand can follow the fork in one run, while the other must restart repeatedly. The tempting belief that both strands grow in one piece fails because antiparallel geometry forbids it, and the belief that reading and building run the same way fails because the first fixes the second.
questions.hint: Decide which direction the new strand's growing end can travel.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Okazaki Fragments
questions.learningObjective: identify the short pieces made on the lagging strand and how they are joined
questions.stem: On one side of a moving replication fork the new strand is built as a series of short pieces, each beginning with its own starter, and these are later stitched into one long strand. What are the short pieces called?

options.text: Okazaki fragments, joined into a continuous strand once their primers are removed
Leading fragments, joined into a continuous strand once the fork passes them
options.misconception: calls the discontinuous pieces on the continuous side

options.text: Nucleotide primers, joined into a continuous strand once they are extended
options.misconception: treats the starter pieces as the whole of the product

options.text: Base-pair stacks, joined into a continuous strand once bases hydrogen-bond
options.misconception: confuses a covalent fragment with a pair of paired bases

questions.explanation: The short pieces are Okazaki fragments: each begins with its own primer, is extended away from the fork, and then the primers are cut out, the gaps filled with DNA, and the remaining nicks sealed to give one continuous strand. The tempting belief that the primers themselves become the lagging strand fails because a primer is only a few bases long and is removed, and the label leading fragments fails because the leading strand is precisely the one that is not made in pieces.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the fork cannot be copied in one run.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Unwinding the Duplex
questions.learningObjective: identify the enzyme that separates the parental strands and the bonds it breaks
questions.stem: One enzyme uses chemical energy from ATP to pull the two parent strands apart at the fork so that the template bases become accessible. Which enzyme is doing that, and which bonds does it break?

options.text: Helicase, breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold complementary bases together
DNA polymerase, breaking the hydrogen bonds as it adds the first nucleotide
options.misconception: credits the copying enzyme with unwinding the duplex

options.text: Primase, breaking the hydrogen bonds as it lays down the first RNA primer
options.misconception: credits the priming enzyme with unwinding the duplex

options.text: Ligase, breaking the hydrogen bonds as it joins two fragments into one
options.misconception: credits the sealing enzyme with unwinding the duplex

questions.explanation: Helicase is a motor protein that hydrolyses ATP to force the parental strands apart, and the only bonds it must break are the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which is why separation costs little and is easily reversed. The tempting belief that the polymerase, primase, or ligase does the unwinding fails because their substrates are new strand ends, primer starts, and nicks rather than paired bases, and the belief that covalent links inside a strand must be cut fails because each backbone stays intact throughout replication.
questions.hint: Ask which enzyme's substrate is a pair of hydrogen-bonded bases.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Proofreading at the Growing End
questions.learningObjective: identify the exonuclease check performed by a copying polymerase
questions.stem: A diagram shows a polymerase extending a new strand, with the most recently added nucleotide drawn as a mismatched pair. The enzyme is then shown stepping back, that nucleotide being removed, and the correct one inserted in its place. Which proofreading activity is being pictured?

options.text: A three-prime to five-prime exonuclease check on the newly added nucleotide
A five-prime to three-prime exonuclease check on the newly added nucleotide
options.misconception: confuses proofreading with the later primer-removal direction

options.text: A ligase seal that converts the mismatch into a correct pair before moving on
options.misconception: credits the sealing enzyme with proofreading a base

options.text: A helicase reset that un-mismatches the pair by re-pairing the parent strands
options.misconception: credits the unwinding motor with error correction

questions.explanation: The picture is a proofreading exonuclease activity that works on the new strand from its three-prime end, the only place a wrong base can be removed while synthesis is still in progress, after which the polymerase resumes from the corrected end. The tempting belief that proofreading runs five-prime to three-prime confuses it with the separate later activity that removes primers, and the belief that ligase corrects bases fails because ligase only seals a nick between two pieces that are already correct.
questions.hint: The check can only act where the chain is still growing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: The End Replication Problem
questions.learningObjective: explain how telomerase protects the ends of a linear chromosome
questions.stem: At the end of a linear chromosome the last starter cannot be replaced from a template, so a little sequence is lost from each round of copying. How does a cell that divides many times keep its gene-containing ends from shrinking away?

options.text: Telomerase, which uses its own RNA template to add DNA to the chromosome end
DNA ligase, which adds extra nucleotides to the end without using any template
options.misconception: thinks the sealing enzyme can invent new sequence

options.text: DNA polymerase, which copies the end twice so the second copy becomes permanent
options.misconception: believes one end can serve as template for its own repair

options.text: Mismatch repair, which restores missing bases wherever a strand is short
options.misconception: confuses gap filling with rebuilding a whole lost end

questions.explanation: Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase that carries an RNA template inside itself and uses it to add a short repeat sequence to the three-prime end of the chromosome, so the lost bases are replaced instead of shaved away and the gene-bearing sequence beside the repeat is preserved. The tempting belief that ligase invents sequence fails because ligase seals breaks using ends that already exist, and the belief that copying the end twice helps fails because there is no second template out at the terminus to copy from.
questions.hint: Ask which enzyme here builds DNA from an RNA, and where that RNA comes from.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Time Needed to Copy a Genome
questions.learningObjective: compute how long replication takes from genome size and fork speed
questions.stem: A bacterium has a circular genome of 5,000,000 base pairs and starts one round of replication from a single origin, with two forks travelling in opposite directions. Each fork copies 1,000 nucleotides per second. How many seconds does it take to copy the whole genome?

options.text: 5,000 seconds
options.misconception: ignores the two forks and lets one copy the whole circle

options.text: 2,500 seconds
1,250 seconds
options.misconception: assumes four forks travelling instead of two

options.text: 10,000 seconds
options.misconception: doubles the genome length before dividing by fork speed

questions.explanation: Each fork covers half the circle, so each copies 2,500,000 nucleotides, and 2,500,000 divided by 1,000 per second is 2,500 seconds. Back-substitution agrees: two forks at 1,000 nucleotides per second for 2,500 seconds build 5,000,000 nucleotides, which is exactly the 5,000,000 base pairs of the genome, so the genome is complete. The tempting wrong belief is that one fork copies the whole circle, which would give 5,000 seconds and is the usual single-origin error.
questions.hint: Each fork only covers half of a circle that begins at one origin.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Coding Sequences: Length from Protein Length
questions.learningObjective: convert a protein length into a coding nucleotide count
questions.stem: A small protein contains 250 amino acids, counting the starting methionine as the first one, and translation ends at a stop codon that is not part of the protein. How many nucleotides of coding sequence are needed, from the start codon through the stop codon?

options.text: 747 nucleotides
options.misconception: counts the residues but forgets to add the stop codon

options.text: 750 nucleotides
options.misconception: multiplies residues by three and omits the stop codon

options.text: 753 nucleotides
1,003 nucleotides
options.misconception: adds a start codon on top of the stop codon

questions.explanation: Each residue is specified by one codon of three nucleotides, so 250 residues take 250 times three, which is 750 nucleotides, and the stop codon adds three more for 753. Counting codons instead of residues gives the same figure: one codon per residue plus one stop makes 251 codons, and 251 times three is again 753. The tempting wrong belief is that a protein of 250 residues needs exactly 750, which forgets that the stop signal is itself written into the sequence even though it encodes no amino acid.
questions.hint: A chain of n residues needs n codons plus one stop codon.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Copying Fidelity: Error Rate Scaled to a Genome
questions.learningObjective: scale a per-nucleotide error rate to whole-genome error counts
questions.stem: A mutant polymerase leaves one wrong base for every 10,000 nucleotides it adds. It copies a genome of 4,000,000 base pairs, so 8,000,000 fresh nucleotides are built into the two new strands, and no repair acts afterwards. How many mismatched base pairs should the finished double helix contain?

options.text: 40 mismatched pairs
options.misconception: divides the genome length by the error rate twice over

options.text: 400 mismatched pairs
options.misconception: counts errors on one new strand and forgets the other

options.text: 800 mismatched pairs
8,000 mismatched pairs
options.misconception: reads the error rate as one error per thousand nucleotides

questions.explanation: Both new strands are newly synthesised, so 4,000,000 base pairs means 8,000,000 nucleotides are added, and 8,000,000 divided by 10,000 per error is 800 errors. The same count follows strand by strand: each new strand is 4,000,000 nucleotides, which gives 400 errors, and the two strands together give 800, one error per duplex. The tempting wrong belief that 400 is the answer forgets that a base pair needs two newly made halves before it can be mismatched.
questions.hint: Both new strands are new, so count nucleotides rather than base pairs.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Lagging Strand: Counting Primers
questions.learningObjective: count primers from template length and fragment length
questions.stem: The template that is copied in fragments on the lagging side is 3,000 nucleotides long, and each finished fragment is 200 nucleotides. Every fragment, including the last one, needs its own starter laid down first. How many primers are placed on that template?

options.text: 15 primers
20 primers
options.misconception: multiplies the two numbers instead of dividing them

options.text: 14 primers
options.misconception: assumes the last fragment needs no starter of its own

options.text: 30 primers
options.misconception: counts a primer at both ends of every fragment

questions.explanation: A 3,000 nucleotide template carries 3,000 divided by 200, which is 15 fragments, and one primer is laid down to start each fragment, so 15 primers are needed. Counting primers instead of fragments agrees: every primer is followed by DNA that extends up to the next primer, so the number of primers equals the number of fragments. The tempting wrong belief that 14 are enough fails because the final fragment also has to be begun, and 3,000 into 200 leaves no partial remainder to hide a sixteenth.
questions.hint: One primer per fragment, so count the fragments first.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Messenger RNA Decay: Reading a Half-Life
questions.learningObjective: extract a half-life from a decay series and predict another value
questions.stem: The amount of a particular messenger RNA in a sample falls from 80 nanograms to 5 nanograms over 40 minutes, and the loss is steady rather than sudden. Treating the decay as repeated halving, how many minutes would it take to go from 80 nanograms down to 10 nanograms?

options.text: 20 minutes
options.misconception: assumes one halving per ten minutes without reading the data

options.text: 30 minutes
40 minutes
options.misconception: copies the full 80 to 5 drop instead of the 80 to 10 drop

options.text: 10 minutes
options.misconception: counts the number of halvings as if it were the time

questions.explanation: Dropping from 80 to 5 nanograms is a sixteen-fold fall, which is four halvings, so four halvings take 40 minutes and one halving takes 10 minutes. Dropping from 80 to 10 nanograms is an eight-fold fall, which is three halvings, and three times 10 minutes is 30. The same result comes from a rate constant: the decay constant is 2.772 divided by 40 minutes, about 0.069 per minute, and 2.079 divided by 0.069 is again 30 minutes. The tempting wrong belief that 80 to 10 is four halvings confuses an eight-fold fall with a sixteen-fold one.
questions.hint: 80 to 5 is a sixteen-fold fall, so count the halvings in both drops.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Inferring the Start Time
questions.learningObjective: work backwards from transcript length and rate to a start time
questions.stem: A cell finishes exporting a messenger RNA of 1,200 nucleotides at a clock reading of 4 minutes, and the enzyme copies at 30 nucleotides per second. How many seconds before that export was observed did the copying enzyme actually start?

options.text: 200 seconds
240 seconds
options.misconception: uses the export time without subtracting the copying time

options.text: 280 seconds
options.misconception: adds the copying time to the export time instead of subtracting

options.text: 40 seconds
options.misconception: gives only the time spent copying, ignoring the export lag

questions.explanation: Copying 1,200 nucleotides at 30 per second takes 1,200 divided by 30, which is 40 seconds, so transcription began 40 seconds before it finished. Export was observed 4 minutes, or 240 seconds, after transcription began, so the enzyme started 240 minus 40, which is 200 seconds, before the export. The same figure falls out by adding forward: 200 seconds of waiting plus 40 seconds of copying gives the 240 second interval that was measured, so the start sits 200 seconds back.
questions.hint: Work out how long the copying itself took, then subtract that from the export time.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Sequencing the Events at a Fork
questions.learningObjective: order the events of replication from unwinding to sealing
questions.stem: A bacterial cell is copying its genome and you are watching one replication fork. Put these five events in the order in which they happen as that fork advances along the DNA.

options.text: A single nucleotide is checked and any wrong one is cut back off
options.misconception: running the proofreading check before any base is added

options.text: The two parent strands are pulled apart at the replication origin
options.misconception: unwinding only after the new chain has begun

options.text: Short RNA primers are laid down wherever a new strand must begin
options.misconception: priming after the chain is complete, with nothing to extend

options.text: Primers are removed, replaced with DNA, and the nicks are sealed
options.misconception: cleaning up before the new chain has been built

options.text: Bases are added opposite the template bases that are now exposed
options.misconception: adding bases before any primer is available to extend

questions.hint: Unwinding, then a start, then building, then checking, then tidying.

questions.topic: Gene Expression: From DNA to a Working Protein
questions.learningObjective: order transcription, processing, export and translation
questions.stem: Follow one eukaryotic gene from the moment its DNA is first copied to the moment a working protein appears in the cytosol. Put these four steps in the order they must occur.

options.text: A spliceosome removes the introns and joins the surviving exons
options.misconception: cutting the message before it has been copied at all

options.text: A cap is added to the front and a poly-A tail to the back
options.misconception: adding the caps before the transcript is copied

options.text: A ribosome reads the exported message and links amino acids together
options.misconception: translating a message that is still being copied on DNA

options.text: The copying enzyme reads the template strand into a pre-mRNA
options.misconception: assuming the final message is copied straight from DNA

questions.hint: Nothing can be edited or read until the first copy exists.

questions.topic: Transcription: The Promoter
questions.learningObjective: identify the DNA sequence that signals where transcription starts
questions.stem: Transcription begins when the enzyme that copies RNA settles onto a specific DNA sequence just upstream of a gene, opens about a dozen base pairs, and starts making RNA. What is that DNA sequence called?

options.text: The promoter, the DNA sequence the copying enzyme recognises to begin
The terminator, the DNA sequence that halts the enzyme at the gene's end
options.misconception: names the stopping signal as the starting signal

options.text: The start codon, the three-letter signal the enzyme reads on the transcript
options.misconception: mislocates the start signal from DNA onto RNA

options.misconception: confuses transcription start with replication start

questions.topic: Transcription: Template and Coding Strands
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the template strand from the coding strand
questions.stem: A diagram shows a gene drawn as two labelled strands. An arrow runs along the bottom strand in words as three prime to five prime, and a new RNA strand is being built against it. options.text: Bottom is the template, read three to five prime; the top is the coding strand
Bottom is the coding strand, read three to five prime; the top is the template
options.misconception: swaps which strand is actually copied

options.text: Bottom is the template, read five to three prime; the top is the coding strand
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which the template is read

questions.topic: RNA Processing: Introns and Exons
questions.learningObjective: name the removed and retained parts of a pre-mRNA
questions.stem: A pre-mRNA from a human gene contains long stretches that are absent from the mature message, plus shorter stretches that remain and end up joined together. What are the removed stretches called, and what removes them?

Exons, removed by a spliceosome before the message leaves the nucleus
options.misconception: swaps the retained and discarded parts of the transcript

options.misconception: credits translation machinery with RNA splicing

questions.topic: Translation: Codon and Anticodon Pairing
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a codon pair with one transfer RNA
questions.stem: A diagram shows a strip of messenger RNA running left to right with three bases in a row marked as a codon. Opposite it sits a transfer RNA drawn as a folded shape, and at the end facing the strip is a small three-base loop marked as the anticodon. What makes this pairing the correct one?

options.text: The two triplets are complementary and opposed in the right direction
The two triplets are identical and read in the same order as written
options.misconception: believes a codon pairs with an RNA of the same sequence

options.text: Any three bases will do, so one transfer RNA reads a whole codon family
options.misconception: believes codon pairing is loose and interchangeable

options.text: Only the last base of each triplet is checked, so any family is read alike
options.misconception: reduces codon recognition to the third base alone

questions.explanation: The anticodon is complementary to the codon and lies antiparallel to it, so adenine on one side lines up with uracil and guanine with cytosine on the other, which is what makes the match specific enough for the ribosome to test it. The tempting belief that the two must be identical fails because identical triplets could not distinguish a codon from its own complement, and the belief that any three bases will pair fails because a mis-paired transfer RNA would deliver the wrong amino acid and the synthetase check has already been passed by then.
questions.hint: Ask what a base pairs with, not what it looks like.

questions.topic: Translation: The Ribosome Sites
questions.learningObjective: name the ribosome slots that unload and accept transfer RNAs
questions.stem: A diagram of a ribosome shows two subunits with three slots in a row between them. In the middle slot sits a transfer RNA carrying the growing chain, in the next slot to one side an empty transfer RNA has just arrived holding a new amino acid, and in the far slot an unloaded transfer RNA is leaving. What are the two outer slots called, and what do they do?

options.text: The E and A sites, which unload departing RNAs and accept arriving ones
The A and P sites, which unload departing RNAs and accept arriving ones
options.misconception: names the two occupied slots as the outer ones

options.text: The E and P sites, which unload departing RNAs and accept arriving ones
options.misconception: leaves out the slot where new amino acids are handed over

options.text: The P and R sites, which unload departing RNAs and accept arriving ones
options.misconception: invents a slot that no ribosome actually has

questions.explanation: The exiting slot, called E, is where an unloaded transfer RNA leaves after handing over its amino acid, and the aminoacyl slot, called A, is where a charged transfer RNA arrives and is tested against the next codon, while the P slot in the middle holds the chain. questions.hint: Name the slot each transfer RNA enters by, and the one it leaves by.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Information Flow: The Usual Direction and Its Exception
questions.learningObjective: state the usual direction of information flow and name a documented reversal
questions.stem: In most organisms information is used in a fixed sequence from DNA to RNA to protein, but a documented exception runs the other way for part of a cycle. Which pair states the usual flow and that exception correctly?

options.text: DNA to RNA to protein, with reverse transcription back to DNA as the exception
Protein to RNA to DNA, with transcription to RNA as the exception
options.misconception: runs the sequence backwards and calls the usual step an exception

options.text: DNA to protein directly, with RNA as an exception that carries the instructions
options.misconception: skips the RNA step in the normal direction of flow

options.text: RNA to DNA to RNA, with protein as an exception that carries the instructions
options.misconception: makes the intermediate product rather than the protein the template

questions.explanation: The sequence a cell generally uses is DNA to RNA to protein, with a few viruses documented as reversing the first step by copying their RNA genome back into DNA and inserting it into the host genome, so the arrow can point from RNA to DNA. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: DNA Replication: Reading a Density Gradient Test
questions.learningObjective: interpret a density gradient result after two generations of replication
questions.stem: Bacteria were grown for many generations in medium containing only the heavy form of nitrogen, then moved into medium containing only the light form. After two more generations their DNA was separated on a density gradient. Which reading of the result matches semiconservative replication, and why?

options.text: Two bands, one intermediate and one light, each holding about half the DNA
One band at intermediate density, because every molecule mixes one old and one new strand
options.misconception: gives the result of the first generation and not the second

options.text: Two bands, one heavy and one light, because the old duplexes stayed intact
options.misconception: reports the pattern a conservative model would give

options.text: One band at heavy density, because no light nitrogen was taken up at all
options.misconception: assumes the cells refused the new nitrogen source

questions.explanation: After one generation every molecule is a hybrid holding one old heavy strand and one new light strand, so the single intermediate band seen at that point already fits semiconservative replication. After a second generation each hybrid template produces one hybrid duplex and one all-light duplex, so the gradient shows an intermediate band and a light band in equal measure, which is the reading offered here. The tempting belief that one intermediate band persists forever fails because that pattern describes generation one, and the belief that a heavy band survives fails because no old-old duplex is ever rebuilt.
questions.hint: Work out what a second round of copying does to the hybrids already present.

questions.topic: RNA: Following a Pulse of Labelled Nucleotide
questions.learningObjective: state what a pulse and chase adds to a single time point
questions.stem: Cells are given a short labelled pulse of nucleotides and then chased with unlabelled ones. The total mass of RNA in the cell, which needs measurements over time
options.misconception: confuses tracking a labelled subset with weighing all the RNA

options.text: Which genes are switched on, which needs measurements over time
options.misconception: overreads a pulse-chase as a test of which genes are active

questions.topic: Gene Expression: Reading a Reporter Construct
questions.learningObjective: interpret what a reporter gene reports and what it does not
questions.stem: A researcher replaces the coding region of a gene with a marker that makes a glowing protein, leaves the original regulatory DNA in place, and measures glow in several tissues. What does the level of glow in each tissue actually report?

options.text: How hard that gene's promoter is being read there, not the native protein's amount
How much of the native protein is present there, since the marker replaces it exactly
options.misconception: assumes the substitute protein behaves identically in every respect

options.text: How many copies of the gene each tissue carries, since glow scales with copy number
options.misconception: reads a regulatory readout as a measure of gene number

options.text: How stable the native protein is, since the marker shares its original folding
options.misconception: assumes the substitute protein has the same turnover rate

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Gene Function: What a Knockout Result Shows
questions.learningObjective: state the conclusion a knockout phenotype supports and does not support
questions.stem: Researchers delete a gene in mice. The animals grow, breed, and behave normally in the tests used, and the gene's RNA is gone from every tissue examined. Which conclusion is properly supported by that result?

options.text: The gene is not needed for these functions under these conditions, not that it is useless
The gene never mattered, since removing it changed nothing that was measured
options.misconception: generalises one battery of tests into a claim of no function

options.text: The gene must be required elsewhere in life, since these mice managed without it
options.misconception: infers a hidden function from an absence of any observed defect

options.text: The gene affects only behaviour, which the tests used here could not measure
options.misconception: invents a specific untested function to explain a null result

questions.hint: Separate what was tested from what was not.

questions.topic: RNA Surveillance: Premature Stop and Breakdown
questions.learningObjective: explain why a premature stop lowers message abundance without lowering transcription
questions.stem: A single base change turns a coding triplet into a stop codon early in a gene. Sequencing shows far less full-length messenger RNA than in normal cells, while the measured rate at the promoter is unchanged. What best accounts for the shortfall?

options.text: The premature stop marks the message for breakdown rather than lowering transcription
The stop codon now blocks the promoter, so the gene cannot be opened
options.misconception: believes a codon in the transcript can shut the DNA promoter

options.text: The copying enzyme now uses the other strand, producing the opposite message
options.misconception: believes one base change switches which DNA strand is transcribed

options.text: The finished message is stuck in the nucleus, because splicing waits for a stop
options.misconception: believes exon joining is triggered by a stop codon

questions.hint: The transcription rate is fixed by the data, so the loss has to be downstream.

questions.topic: DNA Binding: Interpreting a Factor-Binding Profile
questions.learningObjective: interpret a factor-binding profile as physical occupancy rather than output
questions.stem: In one experiment a labelled transcription factor is chemically stuck to the DNA it is sitting on, the chromatin is sheared into short fragments, and the fragments carrying that factor are pulled down with an antibody and sequenced. Sharp peaks of reads appear over a handful of short DNA stretches. What do those peaks establish, and what do they leave open?

options.text: Where the factor is bound on the DNA, not whether the gene is being copied
Where the gene is being copied right now, not where DNA is bound
options.misconception: reads a binding map as a direct readout of transcription rate

options.text: Where the gene is switched off, since binding is part of shutting down
options.misconception: treats every DNA-bound factor as a repressor

options.text: Where the chromatin is fully open, since only open DNA can be cut
options.misconception: assumes shearing fragments reports chromatin accessibility

questions.learningObjective: identify the parts of an inducible operon and its switch

What kind of arrangement is this, and how is it switched?

A repressible operon, held off by a repressor until its product accumulates
options.misconception: switches the logic of the repressor from substrate to product

options.text: An inducible operon, held off by an activator until its substrate appears
options.misconception: makes the blocking protein an activator and reverses the effect

options.text: A regulon, held off by a repressor that binds the finished messenger RNA
options.misconception: places the regulatory binding site on the RNA instead of the DNA

questions.topic: Gene Regulation: A Second Signal Raising Output
questions.learningObjective: explain why a second binding protein raises transcription of an operon
questions.stem: A different protein binds DNA near the same operon's promoter only when the cell's glucose level is low, and while it is bound the amount of transcript made rises sharply. Why is that arrangement worth having?

options.text: It raises output when a sugar is present but the preferred fuel is scarce
It raises output when both sugars are plentiful, so spare sugar is used faster
options.misconception: makes the second signal switch on when there is least need

options.text: It lowers output whenever any sugar is present, saving the enzymes for later
options.misconception: treats a factor that raises transcription as one that lowers it

options.text: It replaces the repressor, so the binding site can never be occupied
options.misconception: believes two regulators cannot both work on one promoter

questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Amount of Enzyme versus Activity
questions.learningObjective: distinguish regulating how much enzyme is made from regulating how well it works
questions.stem: A cell can hold an enzyme in check in two quite different ways, by changing how much of the enzyme it makes or by changing how well the enzyme already present works. Which pairing describes each correctly?

options.text: Gene regulation sets the amount, feedback inhibition sets the activity of what is made
Gene regulation sets the activity, feedback inhibition sets how much is produced
options.misconception: swaps which mechanism acts on amount and which on activity

options.text: Both act on the amount, and neither can slow an enzyme already present
options.misconception: denies that an existing enzyme's activity can be regulated

options.text: Both act on activity, and neither can change how much is produced
options.misconception: denies that a cell can change how much enzyme it makes

questions.learningObjective: explain how a distant DNA site can raise transcription at a promoter

Blocking the promoter by holding the DNA away from the copying enzyme
options.misconception: assumes every distant factor is a repressor

options.text: Replacing the copying enzyme, which cannot reach a gene from so far away
options.misconception: believes a loop substitutes for the copying enzyme

questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Wrapping DNA and Adding an Acetyl Tag
questions.learningObjective: explain how adding an acetyl group loosens DNA from protein cores
questions.stem: A diagram shows DNA drawn as a ribbon wrapped twice around a cluster of small protein spheres, with a small tag labelled acetyl hanging off some of the spheres. A second panel shows the same ribbon with the tags missing and pressed tightly against the spheres. Why does the tagged version allow more transcription?

options.text: The tag removes the core's positive charges, weakening its grip on the DNA
The tag adds negative charge to the DNA, pushing the cores further away
options.misconception: puts the added charge on DNA instead of on the protein core

options.text: The tag breaks the covalent links inside DNA so the ribbon can unwind
options.misconception: confuses loosening chromatin with breaking the backbone

options.text: The tag turns the cores into ribosomes that build the messenger RNA
options.misconception: turns a chromatin core into a translation machine

questions.topic: Gene Regulation: Needing Several Factors at Once
questions.learningObjective: name the principle that several factors together set whether a gene is read

Allosteric control, where several factors must be present before it is read
options.misconception: borrows a term for changes in a protein's own shape

options.text: Feedback control, where several factors must be present before it is read
options.misconception: confuses several inputs with a loop back from the output

questions.learningObjective: explain why messenger RNA and protein amounts need not track each other

The neighbour has no DNA copy, so its message can never reach a ribosome

Codons are read one base at a time, so a lost base removes one amino acid

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Copying Fidelity: Why a Second Repair System Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: explain why proofreading cannot handle errors left behind after synthesis
questions.stem: A copying enzyme checks each nucleotide as it adds it and removes a wrong one about half the time, yet a cell also carries a separate repair system that finds wrongly paired bases later. Explain why proofreading alone cannot be enough, referring to where each check acts.

answer.exemplar: Proofreading works only at the three-prime end of the strand that is still being built, because that is the only place a newly added base can be removed and replaced before it is sealed in. Once synthesis has moved on, a wrong base is paired with a correct one and the polymerase has no way to tell which of the two is at fault from inside its own active site, so the error is left in the product. A separate system then compares the finished strand against the template, using the fact that the new strand is interrupted and chemically distinguishable, identifies the mismatched base, and cuts it out so that filling and sealing can restore the correct pair. The tempting belief that proofreading is not accurate enough explains the wrong thing: the enzyme is highly accurate, it is simply out of reach once the strand has been closed.

questions.explanation: The key point is positional, not quantitative. Proofreading needs a free three-prime end to grip, and once the enzyme has moved on, the wrong base sits opposite a right one with no local signal saying which is which. A later repair system can still use the newer strand as the reference, so the two mechanisms are complementary rather than redundant, and a cell that relied on proofreading alone would carry every error that escaped it permanently.
questions.hint: Ask what a proofreading enzyme has hold of, and whether it still has hold of it later.

questions.topic: RNA Processing: The Poly-A Tail
questions.learningObjective: explain how the tail is made and what it does for a message
questions.stem: A tail of about two hundred adenine bases is added to the back of a eukaryotic message shortly after transcription begins, and no DNA sequence codes for it. Explain how it can be made without a template and why the cell bothers.

answer.exemplar: The tail is added by an enzyme that works without reading DNA, using adenine nucleotides already present in the cell, so the same tail can be placed on many different messages without needing a separate gene for each. Its length is what makes it useful: a long run of the same base is hard for the enzymes that shorten a message to act on, and proteins that bind a message by that feature hold it more firmly and help it leave the nucleus. The tempting belief that the tail must be copied from the gene fails because the tail is not present in the DNA, and the belief that it tells the ribosome where to start fails because that signal sits at the front of the message rather than the back.

questions.explanation: Two ideas carry this item. First, the tail is built enzymatically rather than transcribed, which is why the same tail can decorate messages for thousands of different genes. Second, its function is largely structural and protective, lengthening the life of a message and assisting its export, rather than carrying start information, which lives at the opposite end of the molecule.
questions.hint: Ask what is missing from the gene, and where on a message the start signal sits.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Building Blocks: Why DNA Carries Thymine
questions.learningObjective: explain the repair advantage of thymine over uracil in DNA
questions.stem: A cytosine in DNA can lose an amino group and turn into uracil, which is one of the four bases RNA uses and one that would pair with adenine perfectly well. Explain why using thymine instead of uracil in DNA is worth the cost of making an extra base.

answer.exemplar: The cost is that a cell must make and repair one extra base, and the benefit is that a damaged cytosine is then chemically distinct from a normal base, because a uracil sitting in DNA is something that does not belong there and is recognised and excised by a dedicated enzyme. A thymine in the same position produces a different, rarer product that is recognised far less readily, so the common spontaneous change is caught instead of being mistaken for correct sequence. The tempting belief that thymine makes the helix stronger fails because pairing strength is set by hydrogen bonding, which uracil shares with thymine, and the belief that uracil is too large to fit fails because the two bases occupy almost the same space.

questions.explanation: The argument is about detection rather than about fit or strength. Because uracil does not normally occur in DNA, its appearance after deamination is unambiguous evidence of damage, and a repair enzyme can act on that evidence, whereas a thymine left by a rarer change is much harder to spot. That detectability is what pays for the extra synthesis work of making thymine.
questions.hint: Ask which base would look wrong in DNA if it appeared there.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Chromosome Number Across One Replication
questions.learningObjective: explain why a bacterial cell still has one chromosome after it has copied its DNA
questions.stem: A bacterium with one circular chromosome has finished copying its DNA but has not yet divided. Explain why that single cell still contains one chromosome rather than two, and what the two copies are called at this stage.

answer.exemplar: The two products of replication are sister copies joined at a point and not yet separated, so the cell still holds one duplicated chromosome rather than two independent ones, and the doubling only becomes two chromosomes once the cell has divided and the copies have gone to opposite daughters. The tempting belief that copying DNA creates a new chromosome fails because a chromosome is counted as one continuous piece of DNA, and doubling the amount of DNA doubles the number of copies, not the number of chromosomes in a cell that has not yet divided.

questions.explanation: Chromosome number tracks how many separate DNA molecules a cell holds, and the two products of one round of replication are still joined as one duplicated unit, so a bacterium mid-replication is a cell with one chromosome that has two copies. Only separation of the copies and cell division turns that into two cells with one chromosome each, which keeps the count constant from generation to generation.
questions.hint: Separate the amount of DNA from the number of separate DNA molecules.

questions.topic: Gene Expression: Correcting an Inference from Message Level
questions.learningObjective: explain why message abundance does not by itself fix transcription rate

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Experimental Design: Testing a Candidate Regulatory Site
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test of whether a DNA site regulates a gene
questions.stem: A stretch of DNA about three hundred bases upstream of a gene is proposed as a site where a regulatory protein binds. Describe a test of whether the gene really needs that site, and name the comparison that would make the result trustworthy.

answer.exemplar: Change a small number of bases in the proposed site so the protein can no longer bind, leaving the gene and its own promoter untouched, and then measure how much of the gene's message and protein are made. The essential comparison is against an otherwise identical construct in which the site is left unaltered and against a second construct in which the site is replaced by an equal-length sequence of unrelated bases, because the second controls for the possibility that any change of that length alters expression regardless of what was there before. Repeat across independent copies and report the spread, since one measurement cannot separate a real effect from variation. If only the binding-broken construct shows reduced output, the site is needed; if the substituted construct shows the same reduction, the effect belongs to the length or spacing of the DNA rather than to the proposed binding site.

questions.explanation: A good design here needs three things: a specific intervention that removes the proposed function, an unaltered comparison that shows the baseline, and a substitute comparison that controls for the effect of changing the DNA at all. Without the substituted control, any result could be blamed on the act of inserting bases rather than on the site, and without independent repeats a single difference cannot be told from noise.
questions.hint: Ask what else besides the site changed, and what happens if length matters more than sequence.

questions.topic: Experimental Design: Locating a Loss of Expression
questions.learningObjective: design measurements that separate an RNA step from a protein step

answer.exemplar: Measure two things in the same cells and at the same time: the amount of that gene's messenger RNA, and the amount of the protein, and add a third measurement of how much of the message is loaded onto ribosomes. If the message is also halved, the fault lies at the RNA stage, whether that is less transcription or faster breakdown, and a short labelling pulse can separate those two. If the message is normal while the protein is halved, the fault lies after transcription, in translation or in protein breakdown, and supplying a message that bypasses the cell's own transcription separates those as well. Running the same measurements in a reporter construct under the same promoter gives an independent check that does not depend on knowing the native gene's own control sequences.

questions.explanation: The design works by measuring upstream and downstream of the disputed step in the same cells. Because the message and the protein sit in sequence, a drop that appears in both places points upstream and a drop that appears only in the protein points downstream, and only paired measurements can distinguish those two cases, which is why a single measurement of protein amount answers nothing on its own.
questions.hint: Measure the step before the protein as well as the protein itself.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Copying Fidelity: Why DNA Must Be Copied More Accurately
questions.learningObjective: explain the consequence of a copying error at the DNA step
questions.stem: A cell makes far fewer copying errors when it copies DNA than when it copies a short-lived message, and it repairs some DNA mistakes afterwards. Explain why the difference in accuracy matters so much to the organism.

answer.exemplar: A message is a disposable working copy that lives minutes to hours and can simply be made again, so a mistake in one copy is diluted across many later copies and usually costs nothing. DNA is a long-lived archive copied over many divisions, so a wrong base that escapes proofreading and mismatch repair is not diluted, it is written into every message made from that gene afterwards, and it can be passed to offspring, where a single altered letter may change an amino acid for the rest of that protein's life. That asymmetry between a temporary copy and a permanent record is why the replication machinery adds a reading check as each nucleotide is added, and why a second repair system exists to catch what slips through after the strand has been sealed. The tempting belief that both errors are equally serious fails because the two products differ in how many times they are read and in how long they last.

questions.explanation: The whole item turns on lifespan and copy number. A mistake in a temporary message is averaged away by the next batch, while a mistake in DNA is multiplied across every subsequent reading of that gene and can be inherited, so the expected cost of an error is far higher in the archive than in the working copy, and the extra accuracy is worth paying for.
questions.hint: Ask how long each product lasts and how many times it will be read.
